column3: A comparative Jewish-and-associator scene broadens the focus's group contrast, though its subject is hostility rather than life-seeking.
Immediate context frames their conduct as rejecting unwelcome messengers, supplying a deeds-based background for the warning.
The thousand-year span ends in consequence for wrongdoing, directly separating long duration from immunity.
Its thousand-year measure concerns divine administration of time, not a human wish for prolonged life.
The immediate challenge to wish for death forms the sharp contrary to the focus's avid clinging to life.
Death, recompense, and being moved away from the Fire place worldly life under the final outcome.
Associating others with God is joined to seeing punishment and divine power, clarifying one side of the focus's comparison.
Immediate envy of divine favor and humiliating punishment supplies motive and consequence within the same passage.
A different form of intense desire, directed toward guidance, contrasts human eagerness with an outcome not controlled by desire.
Degrees before God and His sight of deeds repeat only the focus's closing accountability.
Their claim of sealed hearts gives nearby context for persistent refusal behind the focus's warning.
The retained contrast route does not clarify life, longevity, punishment, or accountable deeds here.
Repeated blindness and deafness after repentance portray a recurring pattern of failure, with God seeing deeds.
The immediate refusal to wish for death because of what their hands sent forward explains the attachment to life in the next verses.
Intense concern for others is bound to compassion, providing a contrary moral use of eagerness.
A later wish of disbelievers concerns a different regret and adds little to prolonged life.
Immediate refusal of what confirms their own revelation and the recalled killing of prophets deepen the local conduct context.
Years of enjoyment are posed as a limited interval before what follows, supporting the boundary that duration is not acquittal.
Refusal of guidance and forgiveness is set against the arrival of punishment, giving a general consequence pattern.
Recognition followed by rejection supplies immediate context for the passage's portrayal of knowing refusal.
A long prior lifetime functions as evidence about revelation, not as a claim about escaping punishment through age.
The wrongdoer's wish to ransom himself from punishment shows desire cannot purchase distance from its outcome.
The covenant scene and the calf imbibed into hearts add a nearby pattern of unbelief and disobedience.
Long life is paired with reversal in creation, qualifying any assumption that added years preserve human advantage.
Neither vast wealth nor ransom removes punishment after dying in disbelief, a close boundary on imagined escape.
The surrounding warning that harmful learning brings no afterlife share grounds the passage in consequential deeds.
The delayed punishment promise is not broken, while a thousand-year measure relativizes human expectations of time.
It names the associators among communities whose distinctions are decided on the Day of Resurrection.
The nearby calf episode identifies them as wrongdoers, reinforcing the passage's moral rather than merely temporal concern.
Flight from death does not secure mastery over life, but the collective episode is less specific than the focus's lifespan claim.
Association is said to nullify deeds, making the focus's final sight of deeds materially consequential.
The immediate revelation dispute provides pericope context but does not address life-seeking or its limit.
The counted years of earthly stay are revisited from the final horizon, reducing duration to an accountable measure.
Disobedient people wish for obliteration and cannot conceal speech from God, a post-judgment counterpart to futile wishing.
The immediate declaration of enmity toward persistent disbelief continues the local consequence context.
Extended generations serve the disclosure of an absent past, not the focus's contrast between longevity and punishment.
Every extension and reduction of a lifespan is recorded, directly placing long life within divine knowledge and measure.
Clear signs and their rejection continue the immediate account of culpable disbelief.
Years of upbringing are turned into a claim of political debt, a secondary contrary use of duration.
The prophet's intense desire for belief shows another use of eagerness, while belief remains unforced.
Repeated casting aside of covenant supplies nearby evidence of ongoing conduct rather than an isolated act.
The large population count does not add to the focus's issue of an individual's wished-for lifespan.
Universal submission is contrasted with many for whom punishment is due, framing punishment within divine judgment.
Casting God's Book behind their backs continues the immediate pattern of conscious rejection.
An allotted lifespan and a warner establish a sufficient response period before the plea to return is denied.
Repentance deferred until death is excluded, showing that postponement does not repair a life of wrongdoing.
Faith and restraint are called better recompense, offering the local alternative to the conduct under warning.
The life-oath and wandering intoxication give only an indirect contrast to rationally ordered desire.
People of the Book and associators are jointly described as begrudging divine good, clarifying the focus's paired groups.
A bounded span of years marks divine control of events but adds little to personal longevity.
It joins People of the Book and associators in a trial setting, without clarifying the desire for life.
A single night surpassing a thousand months shows that duration alone is not the measure of value.
The verb here concerns maintaining places of worship, not prolonging a lifespan.
Its immense time measure concerns ascent, not the human wish or punishment boundary in the focus.
Human proximity cannot prevent death; God gives life and death and sees deeds.
Associators' appeal to divine will is answered by the messenger's clear delivery, only indirectly related to the focus.
A good life is joined to faithful good action and later recompense, contrasting life itself with life pursued without that horizon.
Divine selection and hearing-seeing do not materially clarify prolonged life or its consequence.
The Ever-Living divine sovereignty contrasts with human dependence and limits on life.
Those in error may be extended until they see the promised punishment, directly separating respite from vindication.
The response to an associator's analogy does not add to the focus's lifespan or punishment claim.
The legal testimony procedure has no meaningful connection to the focus.
The painful punishment statement repeats only a general element already established more specifically.
At death the plea to return exposes the finality that a wished-for extension cannot overcome.
God's knowledge of all movements and sight of deeds broadly echoes the focus's closing without sharpening it.
God stands over every self and what it earns while false partners are challenged, joining association to personal accountability.
Life in retribution presents a distinct legal principle, not the focus's attachment to life.
False deities lack control over death, life, and resurrection, undermining the associator side of the focus's horizon.
People turn to God in harm and then associate after mercy, showing a recurring instability behind association.
Attractive speech about worldly life and a hostile heart offer only a broad contrast to the focus's deeds.
The repeated hundred and thousand are military ratios, unrelated to lifespan or punishment.
A claim to escape punishment is explicitly denied, closely paralleling the focus's denial of being moved away from it.
Its assertion of seriousness has no focused connection to life, association, or accountable deeds.
Even all earthly wealth cannot ransom punishment, another direct limit on attempted escape.
Punishment for obstructing the sacred mosque is a distinct setting with limited explanatory gain.
Divine knowledge of the unseen and sight of deeds repeat the focus's conclusion without added context.
A messenger's lack of knowledge of followers' deeds adds little to God's sight of deeds in the focus.
Recompense for deeds is too general after closer accountability parallels.
God encompassing deeds adds a broad accountability echo but no further clarification.
Associators' deeds are nullified and their Fire-abiding outcome is stated, giving the comparison an explicit consequence.
Faithful deeds receive full reward while arrogant refusal receives painful punishment, preserving the moral alternative.
What is sent ahead is found with God, but it largely repeats the focus's divine sight of deeds.
Every deed is made present, and the doer wishes a far distance from evil, directly exposing futile wishful distancing.
Associators invoke divine will for their conduct and are answered with the precedent of punishment and unsupported conjecture.
The public disavowal of associators preserves repentance as an alternative to the announced painful punishment.
The record leaves no small or great deed uncounted and finds deeds present, specifying the focus's divine sight.
The believer-disbeliever division and divine sight of deeds add only a general echo.
Conditional worship that loses this world and the next is a secondary contrast to life-seeking.
The occurrence of finding a person in a house is unrelated to the focus.
Divine creative power in a Christological dispute does not materially clarify the focus.
Wealth and children do not avail against God, reinforcing that worldly holdings cannot avert the Fire.
Cosmic creation over six days does not clarify the human lifespan claim.
The exchange about mercy and Paradise lacks a focused link to desired longevity or its consequence.
Rejection and concealment of a Book given through Moses offer only distant pericope-related context.
The call to forgiveness and Paradise supplies a general alternative but no specific clarification of the focus.
Its expiation and vengeance setting concerns a different act, with only a generic consequence parallel.
The prohibition on defending treachery does not materially add to the focus.
Avoiding grave prohibitions and receiving expiation offers a general moral alternative to accumulated culpability.
The Jonah episode in this isolated line does not clarify life-seeking, long duration, or punishment.
The command to fear God and obey is too general to add after the closer cards.
It directly joins choosing worldly life over the hereafter to unabated punishment, making it an immediate missing parallel.
Death occurs only by divine permission at a prescribed term, limiting any human wish to extend life.
Death reaches people wherever they are, providing a direct contrary to imagined security in added life.
Two appointed terms place human duration under divine decree rather than personal desire.
The worldly life is diminished against the hereafter, reinforcing the focus's critique of clinging to life alone.
The promise of an eternal tree introduces the deceptive appeal of unending life.
Every community has a fixed term that cannot be delayed or advanced, directly bounding longevity.
Contentment with worldly life rather than the hereafter exposes the value reversal behind excessive attachment to life.
Those satisfied with worldly life and heedless of signs supply a close moral profile of life-centered desire.
An appointed term cannot be postponed or hastened, directly countering control over lifespan.
Seeking only worldly life brings full worldly return but leaves no share in the hereafter.
The next verse makes the later loss and nullified deeds explicit, completing the worldly-choice consequence.
Preferring worldly life to the hereafter and obstructing God's way gives a direct evaluative parallel.
Those facing consequence ask for a brief delay to respond, showing the futility of a postponed response.
Enjoyment and extended hope are left to distract before knowledge arrives, forming a close warning about deferment.
When the appointed term comes, wrongdoers cannot delay or advance it.
Preferring worldly life to the hereafter is explicitly joined to disbelief and its consequence.
A person who wants the immediate world may receive it, yet faces Hell, distinguishing present gain from final outcome.
The promise of eternity and imperishable dominion shows longevity as a site of temptation rather than security.
No human before the messenger was granted permanence; mortality defeats any expectation of endless life.
Every soul tastes death and is tested in life before return, setting life within trial and final accountability.
Death after earthly life states the unavoidable boundary that long duration cannot remove.
Resurrection after death restores the final horizon omitted by a life-centered desire.
The worldly life is diversion while the final abode is the true life, offering a direct value contrast.
No soul knows in what land it will die, reinforcing the limits of human command over life's end.
The angel of death takes souls before their return to God, sharpening the focus's accountability horizon.
God takes souls at death and during sleep, locating life and death under divine disposal.
Whoever seeks the harvest of this world receives some of it but has no share in the hereafter.
A worldly-life claim that time alone destroys them directly contrasts with the focus's divine judgment and sight of deeds.
The agony of death arrives as the reality people sought to avoid.
Death is decreed among people, and they cannot outstrip the decree.
The worldly life is depicted as temporary display and rivalry, qualified by later punishment or forgiveness.
The repeated challenge for Jews to wish for death is the clearest missing parallel to the immediate context of 2:96.
Their refusal to wish for death because of what their hands sent forward directly parallels 2:95 and the focus's deeds.
The death they flee will meet them before return to the Knower who informs them of their deeds.
At death, a person asks for a brief delay to give and become righteous, showing regret over exhausted time.
When a soul's appointed term comes, God does not delay it, directly closing the hope of extension.
Life and death are created as a test of deeds, clarifying why mere duration is not the measure.
Forgiveness is connected with respite only until an appointed term, preserving the limit within any delay.
Love of the immediate world is named as the contrary to attending to the hereafter.
Leaving the hereafter completes the focus's contrast between worldly attachment and final consequence.
They love the immediate and leave a weighty day behind them, a close account of present-centered desire.
Transgression is paired with preferring worldly life, directly identifying the moral direction at issue.
The Fire as the refuge supplies the stated outcome of that worldly preference.
Preferring worldly life gives a concise direct parallel to the focus's excessive life-seeking.
The hereafter is better and more lasting, supplying the missing evaluative contrast.
Rivalry in accumulation distracts until the graves, showing how worldly pursuit runs into death.
Arrival at the graves makes death the boundary of that distraction.
The belief that wealth will make one live forever is an explicit false-security counterpart to the wished-for thousand years.
